query: For high-entropy-alloy bond coats used in thermal barrier coating systems for high-temperature applications, what single intervention could improve coating durability and reliability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Co‐doping high-entropy alloy bond coats with small amounts of Yttrium (Y) and Hafnium (Hf) will improve coating durability and reliability at high temperatures by promoting a more adherent, thermally stable oxide scale that resists spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy bond coats prepared by laser cladding (undoped state)
generation.intervention: Introduce minor amounts of reactive dopants Y and Hf into the high-entropy alloy composition during processing
generation.conditions: High-temperature service conditions (around 900°C) under corrosive environments such as molten salt mixtures (75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl)
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced formation and stabilization of an Al-rich L12 phase within the FCC matrix, which facilitates the development of a continuous and adherent oxide scale
generation.mechanism: The dopants (Y and Hf) exert a reactive element effect that mitigates grain growth and enhances oxidation behavior. This leads to the formation of a denser and more adherent protective oxide layer that resists spallation during thermal cycling and exposure to corrosive salts.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated (undoped) baseline, the Y and Hf co-doped coatings should exhibit a lower fraction of oxide scale spallation (potentially on the order of a 50% reduction in spallation area, though the exact number is uncertain) and improved thermal stability over comparable exposure times.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy bond coats without Y and Hf doping, which develop less adherent oxide scales and exhibit higher rates of spallation under high-temperature corrosive conditions
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected specifically under severe high-temperature (∼900°C) and molten salt (75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl) corrosion environments; under lower temperature or less aggressive conditions, the benefit may be reduced or negligible
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative degree of spallation reduction and the exact interplay of phases (including any secondary effects on the microstructure) remain uncertain due to processing variability and complex phase equilibria in high-entropy systems

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy bond coats via laser cladding: one set with Y and Hf co-doping and one undoped control set. Expose both sets to a high-temperature (900°C) environment in the presence of a corrosive molten salt mixture (75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl) for a fixed duration (e.g., 10 hours) with repeated thermal cycling. After exposure, conduct microstructural analyses using SEM and XRD, and assess the oxide scale adhesion and spallation area.
measurements: Percentage of oxide scale spallation area (via SEM image analysis)
Grain size and phase identification (using XRD)
Adhesion strength of the oxide scale (via mechanical testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y and Hf co-doped coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in the oxide spallation area or improved adhesion (as compared to the undoped control coatings) under the specified high-temperature corrosive conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. In this study, the Y and Hf co-doping did not change the microstructure morphology and phase structure of the coatings but did improve the thermal stability and resistance of the hot corrosion oxide scale spallation, providing a certain amount of data and theoretical support for the application of EHEA coat
